A 18-year-old female presents with recurring right-sided, throbbing headaches occurring every few
weeks for several years. During episodes, she experiences nausea and visual disturbances in the form
of bright spots, finding relief by resting in a dark, quiet room. She reports no associated weakness,
numbness, or tingling. Her past medical history includes acne, hypothyroidism, obesity, and
endometriosis. Current medications are levothyroxine, oral contraceptives, and topical trans-retinoin.
Vital signs show: temperature 97.1°F (37°C), blood pressure 120/82 mmHg, pulse 70/min, and
respirations 10/min. She consumes 2 glasses of wine with dinner several times weekly, has never
smoked, and works as a receptionist. Neurological examination is normal, and head CT reveals no

acute findings. Which medication would be most appropriate for acute treatment of these episodes?
Answer Choices: (A) Sumatriptan (B) Gabapentin (C) Amitriptyline (D) Ergotamine (E) Acetaminophen
with codeine (F) Verapamil (G) Acetazolamide (H) Topiramate (I) Rizatriptan (J) Botulinum toxin
